questions.scenario: A Kotlin function receives `middleName: String?` from a customer record and must return its length, or 0 when there is no middle name.
questions.question: Which expression is idiomatic and safe?
questions.explanation: The safe call returns null when middleName is null, and the Elvis operator supplies the default. `!!` and the cast both throw on null.

questions.scenario: Kotlin code calls a Java method `String getMiddleName()` that sometimes returns null, and assigns it to `val m: String`. It crashes with an NPE.
questions.question: Why didn't the Kotlin compiler prevent this?
options: Java return values are platform types with unknown nullability, so Kotlin trusts the declared type you choose
Kotlin has no null safety for strings
The Java method must be marked open
val cannot hold strings from Java
questions.explanation: Without nullability annotations on the Java side, Kotlin cannot know. Declare it as String? or annotate the Java API (e.g. JSpecify @Nullable) so the compiler can help.

questions.scenario: You need an immutable value type `Money(amount, currency)` in Kotlin with equals/hashCode/toString, plus an easy way to make a modified copy.
questions.question: What should you declare?
options: class Money(var amount: BigDecimal, var currency: String)
data class Money(val amount: BigDecimal, val currency: String) and use money.copy(amount = ...)
questions.explanation: A data class with val properties generates equals, hashCode, toString, componentN and copy, which is the Kotlin equivalent of a Java record with a convenient 'wither'.

questions.scenario: A Java class calls a Kotlin function `fun loadRates(): List<Rate>` that can throw IOException. The Java code compiles without a try/catch, then fails at runtime.
questions.question: Why did the Java compiler not force exception handling?
options: Kotlin has no checked exceptions and does not declare them in bytecode unless the function is annotated @Throws(IOException::class)
Kotlin wraps all exceptions in RuntimeException
Java ignores exceptions from other languages
questions.explanation: Kotlin does not have checked exceptions. Add @Throws(IOException::class) to Kotlin APIs that Java code calls, so Java callers see the throws clause.

questions.scenario: A sealed interface `PaymentMethod` has three data-class implementations. A new `Ussd` implementation is added.
questions.question: What happens to `when (method) { is Card -> ...; is BankTransfer -> ...; is Wallet -> ... }` used as an expression?
options: It silently returns null for Ussd
It stops compiling until a branch for Ussd (or an else) is added
questions.explanation: A when expression over a sealed type must be exhaustive, just like Java 21's switch over a sealed interface. That makes adding a variant a compiler-guided change.

questions.scenario: You want Java code to call a Kotlin companion function as `RateTable.standard()` instead of `RateTable.Companion.standard()`.
questions.question: What do you add?
questions.explanation: @JvmStatic generates a real static method on the outer class. @JvmOverloads is for default arguments; const is for compile-time constants.

questions.scenario: A team asks why Kotlin classes need the `kotlin-spring` compiler plugin in Spring projects.
questions.question: What's the reason?
options: Kotlin classes are final by default, but Spring creates subclass proxies for some annotated classes; the plugin makes those classes open automatically
questions.explanation: Features such as @Transactional and @Configuration use proxies that subclass your class. Kotlin's final-by-default classes would block that; kotlin-spring (all-open) opens classes with Spring annotations.
